sysd-msg-059.title: How to choose a message queue
sysd-msg-059.text: Picking a queue starts with a list of things to compare. They include speed and scalability, reliability (messages are not lost) and durability (messages kept safe over time). They also include ease of setup and management, ecosystem tools, integration with other software, and the protocols and languages supported. Decide the pattern first. Queues give one-to-one delivery and pub/sub lets many consumers subscribe to a topic. Brokers can offer both, while event streaming platforms offer only pub/sub. Those platforms scale more and suit high volumes, but they cannot guarantee delivery or track which consumers received a message. Then match the delivery guarantee to the need: most brokers offer at-least-once, so consumers see duplicates, and exactly-once costs performance and complexity. Most queues give best-effort ordering, while SQS FIFO orders only within a message group. Protocol matters too. JMS is an API, so systems from different vendors are not interoperable, while AMQP is wire-level, so compliant software interoperates. Finally, look at limits and failure handling: a dead-letter queue sets unprocessable messages aside, and SQS caps message bodies at 256KB.

sysd-msg-053.title: The enterprise service bus, and why it fell out of favor
sysd-msg-053.text: One hub that every application talks through sounds tidy. An enterprise service bus is a pattern in which a centralized software component performs integrations between applications. It transforms data models, routes messages and converts communication protocols. In theory this standardizes communication and lets components scale independently and fail without affecting others. In many organizations, though, the bus came to be seen as a bottleneck. A single point of failure can bring down all communications, and a change to one integration can destabilize others. Message brokers are a lightweight alternative at lower cost, as ESBs have fallen out of favor.

sysd-msg-057.title: Locks, waiting and non-blocking queues
sysd-msg-057.text: What happens when two threads want the same queue at once? A blocking algorithm uses locks. If Thread A is suspended while holding the lock, Thread B may wait for arbitrarily long periods and can starve. In the non-blocking alternative, Thread B is told that access is rejected instead of being made to wait, though other threads may still starve through rejections. Wait-free is stronger: all threads complete their tasks within a finite number of steps, which makes it non-blocking plus starvation-free. A non-blocking queue can be built with compare and swap (CAS). With no thread suspension and no lock waiting, latency drops and deadlock cannot occur.

sysd-msg-068.title: A job's trip through a queue
sysd-msg-068.text: Follow one job through a queue and the steps are short. A producer publishes the job to the queue, then notifies the user of the job's status. A consumer later picks the job up, processes it, and signals that it is complete. Until then the message sits in the queue, stored until it has been processed and deleted. Each message is processed only once, by a single consumer.

sysd-msg-071.title: Backpressure: stop a backlog from slowing everything
sysd-msg-071.text: A queue that grows beyond memory slows down just when it is busiest: the result is cache misses, disk reads and even slower performance. Backpressure prevents this by limiting the size of the queue, which maintains a high throughput rate and good response times for the jobs already in it. Once the queue fills up, clients get a server-busy or HTTP 503 status code, which tells them to try again later. They can retry the request at a later time, perhaps with a backoff strategy (see {{ref:sysd-reliab-079}}).

sysd-msg-070.title: Push or pull: who starts the delivery
sysd-msg-070.text: Who starts the hand-off, the queue or the consumer? Most message queues provide both options. Pull means continuously querying the queue for new messages. Push means the consumer is notified when a message is available. Long-polling, described in {{ref:sysd-msg-100}}, allows pulls to wait a specified amount of time for new messages to arrive. Pub/sub topics push their notices out instantly, which removes the need for consumers to poll for new information.

sysd-msg-055.title: Competing consumers share one queue
sysd-msg-055.text: Several workers can drain one queue at once. The competing consumers pattern enables multiple concurrent consumers to process messages on the same message queue. There is no need to configure complex coordination between them. Each message is still processed only once, by a single consumer, as {{ref:sysd-msg-068}} describes. The price is order: the pattern cannot guarantee message ordering.

sysd-msg-054.title: Six named designs for services that exchange messages
sysd-msg-054.text: Services that exchange messages can draw on named designs, and six are worth knowing. Asynchronous request-reply decouples backend processing from clients for long-running tasks, with the API answering HTTP 202 (Accepted) to acknowledge the request. Publisher-subscriber decouples senders from consumers and avoids blocking the sender to wait for a response; {{ref:sysd-msg-060}} treats it in full. Claim check handles large messages by storing the whole payload in a database and transmitting only a reference, which is later used to retrieve the payload. Priority queue lets requests with a higher priority be received and processed more quickly than those with a lower priority. Saga, from {{ref:sysd-scale-005}}, manages data consistency across services that each own a database, without distributed transactions, which are difficult to scale and can hurt performance. Competing consumers, from {{ref:sysd-msg-055}}, lets multiple concurrent consumers process messages from the same channel without complex coordination, but cannot guarantee message ordering.

sysd-msg-060.title: Publish–subscribe: speak to a topic, not to a person
sysd-msg-060.text: In publish–subscribe, a sender does not know who will read its message, and a reader does not know who wrote it. Publishers sort messages into classes, called topics, and send them without needing to know which components will receive them. Subscribers express interest in one or more classes and receive only messages in those classes, without needing to know who the publishers are. The pattern decouples the components that produce messages from those that consume them, and it supports asynchronous, many-to-many communication. A message published to a topic is pushed immediately to all subscribers, which often perform different functions and can each act on it in parallel. This contrasts with queue-based and point-to-point messaging, where producers send directly to consumers; JMS, for one, supports both models. The gain is greater network scalability and more dynamic topologies. The cost is that it can become harder to modify the publisher's logic or the structure of the published data. Compared with synchronous patterns such as RPC, pub/sub gives the highest decoupling. But it can lead to semantic or format coupling that makes systems entangled or brittle over time. Today it is told apart from its in-process cousin, described in {{ref:sysd-msg-141}}, by its emphasis on decoupling, asynchronous messaging and broker-mediated communication across a distributed system.

sysd-msg-137.title: MQTT: publish-subscribe for tiny devices
sysd-msg-137.text: Despite its name, MQTT has no queues. It is a lightweight publish-subscribe network protocol for machine-to-machine messaging, suited to devices with limited resources or network bandwidth, such as Internet of things sensors. It runs over an ordered, lossless transport, typically TCP/IP. Clients connect to a broker, which receives messages from publishers and routes them to subscribers by topic, so devices and server applications stay decoupled. A broker discards a message with no current subscribers unless it is flagged retained. It keeps one retained message per topic and delivers it to each new subscriber immediately. A publisher can register a default message at connect time, which the broker sends to subscribers if it detects an unexpected disconnect. Each connection chooses a quality of service, in increasing order of overhead: at most once, at least once, or exactly once. That guarantee applies between MQTT sender and receiver, not to TCP. Ordering holds only within one client session on one topic, so messages from independent clients can arrive out of order.

sysd-msg-064.title: Why publish–subscribe scales and stays flexible
sysd-msg-064.text: In publish–subscribe the topic is the only thing both sides share. Publishers are loosely coupled to subscribers and need not know they exist, so each side stays ignorant of system topology and works independently. Many systems also decouple the two in time, unlike client-server, where neither side can post or receive while the other is not running. Push delivery through topics removes the need to poll for updates, which brings faster response time and lower delivery latency; {{ref:sysd-msg-070}} compares push with pull. A publisher simply posts to a topic instead of keeping a roster of peers, so subscribers can change, upgrade, multiply or disappear while the system adjusts dynamically. Pub/sub can scale better than client-server through parallel operation, message caching and tree-based or network-based routing. Redundant subscribers can assure delivery with minimal added complexity: an exact duplicate of a logging subscriber can be added without any impact on other equipment. RSS and Atom syndication show pub/sub scaling beyond a single data center. They accept higher latency and no delivery guarantees, so a low-end web server can reach millions of subscribers.

sysd-msg-141.title: The observer pattern, publish–subscribe's in-process cousin
sysd-msg-141.text: The observer pattern is a close relative of publish–subscribe. A subject keeps a list of observers and automatically notifies them of state changes, typically by calling one of their methods. It sets up a one-to-many dependency without tight coupling: observers register and unregister themselves, and the subject only needs to know they implement an update operation. Subject and observers hold direct references with no broker, and notification is typically synchronous, so the pattern suits in-process uses such as GUI toolkits. Publish-subscribe adds a broker, scales to distributed systems, filters by topic and isolates failures, whereas observer failures can affect the subject.

sysd-msg-140.title: NATS: a plain pub/sub server that can add persistence
sysd-msg-140.text: NATS starts as a plain publish-subscribe server and adds persistence only when you ask for it. It is an open-source messaging system under the stewardship of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. The server is written in Go, with client libraries for dozens of languages, and its core design principles are performance, scalability and ease of use. Core NATS is the publish-subscribe server. JetStream is an optional built-in persistence layer that adds streaming, queues, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery, replay, flow control and a key/value store. It replaced the older STAN (NATS Streaming) approach and uses the Raft consensus algorithm for cluster management and data replication.

sysd-msg-065.title: Where publish–subscribe hurts
sysd-msg-065.text: Publish–subscribe's worst problems are a side effect of decoupling. A broker that stops delivering after a specified time cannot guarantee delivery, so assured delivery needs tighter coupling, such as receipt messages from subscribers. A publisher may assume a subscriber is listening when it is not, and may not be told if a subscriber such as a logger fails. It scales well for small networks with low message volume. As nodes and messages grow, instabilities such as load surges and slowdowns limit the maximum scalability. Brokers can be overloaded tracking subscriptions or fooled into notifying the wrong client, and encryption cannot stop authorized publishers from introducing damaging messages.

sysd-msg-062.title: Filtering: how a subscriber gets only what it wants
sysd-msg-062.text: A subscriber rarely wants every message. In publish–subscribe systems subscribers typically receive only a subset, and the process of selecting the relevant ones is called filtering. Topic-based filtering publishes messages to named topics or channels, and subscribers who register for a topic receive all messages published to it. Content-based filtering lets subscribers define constraints on message attributes or content, and a message is delivered only if it matches. Hybrid systems categorize messages by topic and let subscribers apply content-based filters to the messages within those topics.

sysd-msg-063.title: With or without a broker in the middle
sysd-msg-063.text: Who sits between the publisher and the subscriber? In most publish–subscribe systems, a central intermediary such as a message broker or event bus. Subscribers can be registered at build time, with handlers hardcoded as in GUI event handlers. They can be registered at initialization time, with subscriptions in XML configuration or metadata, or added and removed dynamically at runtime. Brokerless systems skip the intermediary: publishers and subscribers discover each other and exchange messages directly. The Data Distribution Service middleware, for one, uses IP multicast and metadata sharing to set up the communication paths.

sysd-msg-052.title: Message broker or event streaming platform
sysd-msg-052.text: A message broker and an event streaming platform can look alike, but they make different trades. Brokers can support two or more messaging patterns, including message queues and pub/sub, while event streaming platforms only offer pub/sub-style distribution. Streaming platforms are designed for high volumes of messages, are readily scalable, and order streams of records into topics stored for a predetermined amount of time. In exchange, they cannot guarantee message delivery or track which consumers have received the messages. They also offer fewer fault-tolerance features such as message resending, and more limited routing and queueing capabilities.

sysd-msg-066.title: What publish–subscribe services add on top
sysd-msg-066.text: Publish–subscribe services usually do more than relay messages. Topics can typically connect to many types of endpoints, such as message queues, serverless functions and HTTP servers. Fanout happens when a message sent to a topic is replicated and pushed to multiple endpoints, which gives asynchronous event notifications that allow parallel processing. These services often provide very high durability and at-least-once delivery by storing copies of the same message on multiple servers. Topics also authenticate applications that try to publish, which allows encrypted endpoints and encryption of messages in transit over the network.

sysd-msg-061.title: One consumer or every subscriber
sysd-msg-061.text: A queue hands each message to one consumer. A topic hands it to everyone who subscribed. Queues hold messages until they are retrieved, whereas topics transfer messages with little or no queuing and push them out immediately. With a queue the sender often knows the destination it sends to. In pub/sub the publisher need not know who uses its information, and subscribers need not know where it comes from. Most messaging systems support both models in their API, for example the Java Message Service.
